paragraphs: The paper studies how to turn high-dimensional, non-negative feature vectors into binary codes for fast similarity search. Such vectors arise when images or documents are represented through counts or frequencies. Because cosine distance compares their directions, the challenge is to create compact codes that preserve the angular relationships useful for retrieval.

The proposed method quantizes data on a sphere, representing directions through a collection of landmarks. The number of landmarks grows exponentially with dimensionality, which supports low-distortion quantization. The authors also provide an efficient way to compute the binary representation despite this large landmark collection. This combination makes a rich quantization scheme computationally usable.

A learned linear transformation further adapts the representation to the input data by reducing quantization error. The resulting codes therefore reflect both the spherical geometry and the particular data being searched. Experiments on image and text retrieval report better performance than the existing methods considered, supporting the usefulness of this approach in those applications.
neurips-2012-angular-quantization-based-.tldr: An efficient spherical quantization scheme learns binary codes that improve image and text similarity retrieval in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Label ranking asks a learner to order a collection of labels. A complete ranking can force the learner to express preferences even when the evidence is uncertain. This paper allows partial abstention: the learner can leave particular pairs incomparable while still ordering pairs for which it has enough confidence.

The method starts with a predicted probability distribution over complete rankings. From that distribution, it obtains the probability that one label precedes another and applies a threshold to decide which preferences to report. The central issue is structural consistency: a collection of individually accepted pairwise preferences must form a valid partial order.

The authors analyze this construction for the Mallows and Plackett-Luce ranking models. They show that thresholding produces proper partial orders in these settings and characterize which kinds of partial orders the models can express. Experiments also demonstrate practical usefulness. The contribution connects uncertainty about rankings to a mathematically coherent way of making selective predictions.
neurips-2012-label-ranking-with-partial-.tldr: Thresholding pairwise preference probabilities lets ranking models abstain selectively while producing valid partial orders in the analyzed settings.

paragraphs: Hierarchical classification organizes labels into broader and narrower categories. In some applications, predictions must reach the leaf nodes because these most specific categories carry stronger meaning than intermediate ones. Enforcing this requirement becomes harder when an example can receive several labels, since the predicted paths must be considered together.

The paper introduces an algorithm for mandatory leaf node prediction that takes the global hierarchy into account. It handles both trees and directed acyclic graphs, allowing a category structure with more than one route to a node. The authors show that a simple greedy algorithm can efficiently maximize the joint posterior probability of all node labels in their formulation.

They also extend the approach to minimize expected symmetric loss, providing another criterion for choosing predictions. Experiments cover real-world datasets with both kinds of hierarchy. The proposed method consistently outperforms the hierarchical and flat multilabel methods considered, indicating that enforcing specific predictions while accounting for the full label structure can be useful.
neurips-2012-mandatory-leaf-node-predict.tldr: A greedy algorithm supports globally informed leaf-level multilabel predictions on both tree and directed acyclic graph hierarchies.

paragraphs: Matrix reconstruction uses available information to estimate a matrix, with regularization controlling which solutions the learning procedure favors. Different matrix norms impose different forms of control. This paper introduces the local max norms, a family that includes established choices such as the max norm, nuclear norm, and weighted or smoothed weighted trace norms.

The key feature is the ability to interpolate between trace-norm regularization and the more conservative max norm. This places several existing approaches within a common family and provides intermediate choices between them. The regularizer can therefore express a broader range of preferences than choosing only one of the established endpoints.

The authors evaluate this interpolation on simulated data and on Netflix and MovieLens ratings data. They report improved reconstruction accuracy relative to the existing matrix norms considered. They also establish learning guarantees for some members of the new family. The empirical and theoretical contributions are complementary: the experiments support the interpolation's usefulness, while the guarantees cover particular new norms.
neurips-2012-matrix-reconstruction-with-.tldr: Local max norms bridge existing matrix regularizers and improve reconstruction accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis seeks a useful low-dimensional approximation to high-dimensional data. When those data contain sensitive information about individuals, publishing the resulting components raises privacy concerns. This paper studies how to approximate PCA under differential privacy, a framework for balancing protection of individuals with the usefulness of released results.

The proposed method explicitly optimizes the utility of its output. This makes the quality of the private approximation a direct part of the method's design. The authors examine both theoretical properties and empirical performance, connecting the question of what privacy permits with the question of how well a private procedure works on real data.

Their experiments show a large performance gap favoring the proposed method over existing methods. The theory further shows that the compared procedures require different amounts of data as dimensionality grows. The new method is nearly optimal with respect to this dimensional scaling. That qualification matters: the near-optimality claim concerns how sample requirements depend on dimension.
neurips-2012-near-optimal-differentially.tldr: A utility-focused private PCA method improves empirical performance and achieves nearly optimal sample-complexity scaling with dimension.

paragraphs: Statistical relational models combine logical descriptions of relationships with probabilistic representations of uncertainty. Their logical structure can contain symmetries that inference algorithms can exploit. This paper brings that idea to blocked Gibbs sampling, which updates groups of variables together, by constructing an approach that works at the first-order representation level.

The method divides the model's first-order atoms into disjoint clusters. Each cluster is chosen so that exact lifted inference takes polynomial time when assignments to all atoms outside it are fixed. This conditional tractability is central: it makes a cluster update manageable while allowing the algorithm to use the model's relational structure.

The authors propose a way to construct these clusters and assess their computational complexity. This supports a principled tradeoff between accuracy and computational cost when choosing the blocks used for sampling. In the reported experiments, lifted Gibbs sampling achieves better accuracy and convergence than the propositional algorithm, supporting the value of exploiting symmetry within block updates.
neurips-2012-on-lifting-the-gibbs-sampli.tldr: Lifted blocked Gibbs sampling exploits relational symmetry through tractable clusters and improves accuracy and convergence in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes reinforcement learning when states vary continuously and future rewards are not discounted. Its central question is how much reward a learner loses while it is still learning to act well. The authors establish sublinear regret bounds, meaning that the cumulative performance shortfall grows more slowly than the learning horizon.

The algorithm combines state aggregation with upper confidence bounds. Aggregation groups states so that the learner can work with a simplified representation of a continuous space. Upper confidence bounds implement optimism about uncertain outcomes, giving the learner a reason to investigate possibilities whose rewards may be better than current observations suggest.

The guarantees rely on an optimal policy satisfying the Poisson equation and on Hölder continuity of rewards and transition probabilities. The continuity assumptions constrain how sharply the environment can change between nearby states, supporting aggregation. Under the stated assumptions, sublinear regret implies that the average shortfall per step decreases as learning continues, giving a theoretical justification for the combined strategy.
neurips-2012-online-regret-bounds-for-un.tldr: State aggregation and optimistic exploration yield sublinear regret for continuous-state, undiscounted reinforcement learning under the stated regularity assumptions.

paragraphs: Boolean satisfiability asks whether a logical sentence admits an assignment that makes it true. Although SAT is NP-complete, instances arising from a particular application may share useful structure. This paper treats the search for solvers suited to such subsets as a learning problem, connecting computational tractability with geometric separation between representations of sentences.

The authors map sentences into a Hilbert space using features computed from their statistics. If those statistics are computable in polynomial time and the mapped sentences have the required margin, they show that a polynomial-time solver exists for that SAT subset within a framework based on the Davis-Putnam-Logemann-Loveland algorithm. The margin is a sufficient condition for this result.

They further show that a perceptron-style rule finds an optimal solver in the studied family with a bounded number of training updates. They construct features computable in linear time and establish margins for important tractable SAT cases. On a hardware-verification task, experiments report an order-of-magnitude improvement over a state-of-the-art solver.
neurips-2012-perceptron-learning-of-sat-.tldr: A margin-based learning framework identifies efficiently solvable SAT subsets and learns solvers with bounded training updates.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning jointly trains a classifier and selects how to combine several base kernels. Conventional regularizers control the vector of mixing weights, but they do not explicitly use information about relationships between kernels. This paper asks how those relationships can guide the choice of weights when learning a predictive model.

Q-MKL replaces the usual norm penalty with a quadratic penalty defined by a positive semidefinite matrix. This allows a desired covariance structure to influence the mixing coefficients. Information about kernel interactions can come from similarities, correlations between prediction errors, or domain knowledge about the features used to build each kernel. The formulation generalizes commonly used one-norm and two-norm objectives.

The authors apply the method to predicting conversion to Alzheimer's disease using several imaging modalities. It outperforms the state-of-the-art methods considered, with reported p-values much smaller than 0.001. This supports using relationships among information sources in that prediction task. The paper also briefly discusses learning-bound implications through Rademacher complexity.
neurips-2012-q-mkl-matrix-induced-regula.tldr: Q-MKL uses a quadratic regularizer to encode relationships between kernels and improves the reported neuroimaging prediction results.

paragraphs: Learning rules that work in unfamiliar situations requires some way to control how strongly a system adapts to its inputs. This paper proposes that noise and synchronization together could provide such regularization in neural systems. The authors develop theoretical and computational arguments for this possibility using coupled computational systems receiving noisy inputs.

In the analyzed setting, noise on the inputs imposes regularization. The important additional ingredient is correlation between noise variables: disturbances affecting different inputs can vary together. When upstream synchronization changes those correlations over time, it can also adjust the degree of regularization. Synchronization therefore supplies a possible way to regulate the effect of noise dynamically.

The resulting qualitative behavior agrees with experimental observations from visual cortex. This agreement connects the proposed computational mechanism to neural behavior without establishing that it is the brain's actual mechanism. The contribution is a plausible account of how coordinated activity could tune learning constraints, supported by theory, computation, and qualitative correspondence with the cited experimental data.
neurips-2012-synchronization-can-control.tldr: Theoretical and computational results suggest that synchronization could tune neural regularization by changing correlations in input noise.

paragraphs: This paper connects a local rule for changing synaptic connections with questions about learning and useful neural communication. It introduces the selectron, a model obtained as a fast-time-constant limit of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons equipped with spike-timing-dependent plasticity. The simplified model makes it possible to analyze aspects of neuronal learning mathematically.

The authors show that selectron spikes encode estimates of reward. They derive an error bound controlled by a spiking margin and the total synaptic weight. Total synaptic strength also affects how useful those spikes are to other selectrons pursuing reward. The analysis therefore links properties of a neuron's connections to both its own output quality and that output's usefulness downstream.

Using these results, the authors propose a regularized form of spike-timing-dependent plasticity. They show that this modification improves robustness when neuronal learning encounters multiple stimuli. The broader contribution is a learning-theoretic route from an analyzable neuron model to a modified plasticity rule, with synaptic strength playing a central role in the reasoning.
neurips-2012-towards-a-learning-theoreti.tldr: An analyzable neuron model links spike quality to synaptic strength and motivates a more robust, regularized plasticity rule.

paragraphs: Direct policy search learns an agent's decision rule directly and has been useful for complicated reinforcement-learning problems. A remaining challenge is choosing the policy model itself. Improving parameters within a chosen model and deciding which model to use are related tasks, but a policy-learning procedure does not automatically provide a model-comparison criterion.

The paper introduces weighted likelihood policy search, which learns a policy through weighted likelihood estimation. This formulation connects direct policy search with statistical inference. The connection matters because it gives statistical techniques a direct role in policy learning, creating a framework in which estimation and comparison of policy models can be considered together.

Building on the idea of an information criterion, the authors develop a measure for comparing policy models using weighted log-likelihood. The contribution thus includes both an efficient policy-estimation method and a model-selection measure expressed within the same statistical formulation. It addresses how a learner can reason about its choice of policy representation as part of direct policy search.
neurips-2012-weighted-likelihood-policy-.tldr: Weighted likelihood policy search connects policy learning to statistical inference and introduces a corresponding criterion for comparing policy models.

paragraphs: Max-product belief propagation is a distributed method for seeking the most probable assignment in a graphical model. A tight linear-programming relaxation can help characterize an optimization problem, but tightness alone does not generally ensure that belief propagation converges or returns the correct answer. This paper addresses that gap for maximum weight matching.

The authors introduce a graph transformation designed to make belief propagation converge. For their matching algorithm, they prove convergence to the correct optimum when the corresponding linear-programming relaxation is tight. That relaxation may include inequalities associated with non-intersecting odd-sized cycles. The guarantee therefore depends on both the proposed construction and the stated tightness condition.

The theory motivates a heuristic that repeatedly modifies the graphical model through cutting-plane steps. This connects a message-passing algorithm to a strategy for strengthening an optimization formulation. In the reported matching experiments, the heuristic performs as well as traditional cutting-plane methods using linear-programming solvers, supporting its practical promise alongside the conditional theoretical result.
neurips-2013-a-graphical-transformation-.tldr: A graph transformation gives a belief-propagation matching algorithm a correctness guarantee when its specified linear-programming relaxation is tight.

paragraphs: Some relationships among three variables are especially apparent when their combined behavior is examined. This paper introduces nonparametric kernel tests for Lancaster three-variable interaction and for total independence. These address related but distinct questions about joint structure, using a framework that represents signed measures in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space.

That representation produces test statistics that are straightforward to compute. For a large family of kernels, the interaction tests are consistent against all alternatives: with increasing data, they can detect departures covered by the testing problem. The result supplies a theoretical foundation for detecting interaction without choosing a fixed parametric form for the variables' relationship.

The Lancaster test is particularly sensitive when two independent causes each have a weak effect on a third variable but exert a strong combined effect. This pattern is relevant to V-shaped structures in directed graphical models. The authors report that their test outperforms competing nonparametric tests at detecting these structures, linking the interaction measure to a concrete structure-discovery task.
neurips-2013-a-kernel-test-for-three-var.tldr: Kernel tests detect three-variable interactions, including strong combined effects that help reveal V-structures in directed graphical models.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to infer hidden roles and latent structure in very large networks using a probabilistic model. The computational challenge is to retain useful information about network organization while making inference feasible at a scale that many existing methods cannot handle. The proposed approach combines a compact representation with efficient statistical learning.

Networks are represented as collections of triangular motifs. This succinct description is paired with a parsimonious statistical model and a stochastic variational inference algorithm. The three components work together: the representation summarizes network structure, the model expresses latent roles, and the inference procedure estimates that structure efficiently.

The authors report analyzing real networks with more than a million vertices and hundreds of latent roles on one machine within hours. Compared with state-of-the-art probabilistic methods, their approach is several orders of magnitude faster while achieving competitive or improved accuracy for latent-space recovery and link prediction. These findings show substantial computational gains without sacrificing accuracy in the reported comparisons.
neurips-2013-a-scalable-approach-to-prob.tldr: A triangular-motif representation and stochastic variational inference make probabilistic latent-role analysis feasible for million-vertex networks.

paragraphs: Many machine-learning methods fit models by minimizing a loss together with a regularization penalty. Stochastic dual coordinate ascent is an effective optimization technique for this setting. This paper extends it to mini-batches, where an update works with a group of coordinates, and introduces acceleration into that setting.

The principal contribution is an accelerated mini-batch algorithm with a proven fast convergence rate. Such a result characterizes how the optimization procedure approaches its solution as it proceeds. Combining acceleration with mini-batch updates is the central design issue: the paper supplies both an algorithmic extension and a theoretical account of its convergence.

The authors also discuss implementing the method on a parallel computing system. They compare its results with standard stochastic dual coordinate ascent and Nesterov's accelerated deterministic gradient descent. These comparisons place the method alongside both a closely related stochastic technique and an established accelerated alternative. The stated contribution connects convergence theory with the practical question of organizing optimization work for parallel execution.
neurips-2013-accelerated-mini-batch-stoc.tldr: An accelerated mini-batch version of stochastic dual coordinate ascent comes with a fast convergence guarantee and a parallel implementation discussion.

paragraphs: A stochastic differential equation describes a system whose evolution combines a systematic tendency with randomness. This paper estimates the drift function, which expresses that systematic tendency, when observations of the system's state are incomplete. The challenge includes both learning the function and accounting for dynamics that are not directly observed.

The authors place a Gaussian process prior over drift as a function of the state vector. This provides a nonparametric approach to estimating the function. They then develop an approximate expectation-maximization algorithm to handle the unobserved dynamics between observations, linking reconstruction of hidden states with estimation of the rule governing their evolution.

Two approximations make up the inference procedure. A piecewise linearized process approximates the posterior distribution over states, while sparse Gaussian process regression supports maximum a posteriori estimation of the drift. Together, these components provide a method for learning stochastic dynamics from partial observations. The contribution is an approximate inference framework that treats uncertainty about hidden trajectories and estimation of the drift within one procedure.
neurips-2013-approximate-gaussian-proces.tldr: An approximate EM method combines latent-state inference with sparse Gaussian process regression to estimate stochastic drift from incomplete observations.

paragraphs: Understanding a neural circuit requires studying how its neurons fluctuate and interact as a population. Calcium imaging can record hundreds of neurons simultaneously, while the circuits involved in computation may contain thousands. This paper addresses the mismatch by combining recordings of different neuron groups collected sequentially from the same circuit.

The method treats these recordings as observations of a shared latent dynamical system with missing data. At any recording period, activity from neurons outside the imaged group is unobserved. Fitting one model across the partial recordings allows information from the separate groups to contribute to a common description of population dynamics.

Using recordings from mouse somatosensory cortex, the authors demonstrate prediction of noise correlations between neuron pairs that were not recorded simultaneously. This is a concrete test of the model's ability to connect separate observations. The approach substantially expands the population sizes whose dynamics can be characterized beyond the number of neurons available in a single simultaneous recording.
neurips-2013-inferring-neural-population.tldr: A shared latent dynamical model combines partial neural recordings and predicts correlations between neurons never recorded together.

paragraphs: Training a deep Boltzmann machine presents difficulties when the model must support useful predictions. Earlier methods either perform poorly on classification or require an initial stage that trains layers greedily, one at a time. This paper introduces the Multi-Prediction Deep Boltzmann Machine as a way to train without that layerwise pretraining stage.

The approach has two complementary interpretations. It is a single probabilistic model trained using a variational approximation to generalized pseudolikelihood. It can also be understood as a family of recurrent networks that share parameters and approximately solve different inference problems. These perspectives connect a probabilistic training objective with several prediction procedures using the same learned parameters.

The authors report better performance than a standard deep Boltzmann machine on classification, classification with missing inputs, and mean-field prediction tasks. The results support the usefulness of training a shared model for multiple inference problems. Alongside those empirical gains, removing greedy pretraining changes the training procedure by eliminating the need for a separate layer-by-layer initialization pass.
neurips-2013-multi-prediction-deep-boltz.tldr: Multi-Prediction Deep Boltzmann Machines avoid greedy layerwise pretraining and improve several prediction tasks over a standard DBM.

paragraphs: High-dimensional models often contain simpler underlying structure, and penalized estimation encourages a fitted model to recover that structure. This paper develops a general theory for penalized M-estimators with a particular geometric form. The goal includes consistency of estimation and model selection consistency, concerning recovery of the appropriate underlying model structure.

The framework applies to geometrically decomposable penalties, which can be written as sums of convex support functions. The authors extend the notion of an irrepresentable condition to this class. This creates a way to express conditions relevant to consistent recovery using the geometry of the penalty, rather than developing an entirely separate analysis for each estimator.

The authors then use the framework to derive results for special cases relevant to bioinformatics and statistical learning. Its value is the common theoretical treatment of structured estimation problems within the specified penalty class. The results provide a framework for establishing consistency under suitable conditions; they do not assert that every penalized estimator automatically recovers the correct model.
neurips-2013-on-model-selection-consiste.tldr: A geometric framework supplies conditions for estimation and model selection consistency across a class of structured penalized estimators.

paragraphs: Binary classification predicts a class, bipartite ranking orders examples, and class probability estimation assigns probabilities to classes. Good probability estimates can support both classification and ranking, but the reverse relationships are less immediate. This paper studies how predictive quality can transfer among these problems using bounds on regret, or excess error.

The authors introduce weak regret transfer bounds. Here, the transformation from a model for one problem to a model for another may depend on the underlying data distribution. This qualification expands the possible connections, but it also means that the required transformation must be estimated from data in practical use.

Within this weaker framework, a good ranking model can produce a good classifier by selecting a suitable score threshold. It can also produce good class probability estimates by calibrating its scores. The latter result gives a stronger role to ranking quality: with an appropriate distribution-dependent conversion, useful ordering information can support probability estimation as well as discrete class decisions.
neurips-2013-on-the-relationship-between.tldr: Distribution-dependent regret bounds show how good rankings can be converted into good classifiers and calibrated probability estimates.

paragraphs: Multilabel classification becomes computationally demanding when the collection of possible labels is large. This paper reduces the problem to binary classification by encoding label sets as low-dimensional binary vectors. The representation draws on Bloom filters, which provide compact representations for approximate membership testing.

A direct application of Bloom filters is vulnerable to errors made by the individual binary classifiers predicting the encoded representation. The authors show this lack of robustness and design an alternative that uses a feature of large real-world label collections: many labels rarely, or never, occur together. This co-occurrence structure becomes part of the approach to reliable compressed prediction.

The resulting method has a robustness guarantee and training and inference complexity that grow sublinearly with the number of labels. It also compares favorably with state-of-the-art algorithms on two large multilabel datasets. The contribution brings compact representation, resistance to prediction errors, and computational scaling into one approach, using label relationships to make the compressed classification task more dependable.
neurips-2013-robust-bloom-filters-for-la.tldr: A robust Bloom-filter-based label encoding uses rare label co-occurrence to support scalable multilabel classification.

paragraphs: An agent that encounters a sequence of tasks may benefit from retaining what it learned earlier. This paper studies that idea in online learning through multi-armed bandits, where an agent repeatedly chooses among actions and learns from the rewards it receives. The setting considers a finite collection of possible task models.

The objective is to minimize cumulative regret across the sequence by transferring knowledge incrementally from earlier tasks. This makes the history of tasks relevant to decisions on later ones. The paper therefore treats transfer as an ongoing component of learning, with the quality of the full sequence of decisions providing the performance criterion.

The proposed bandit algorithm uses a method-of-moments approach to estimate the possible tasks. Those estimates provide the basis for transferring experience as new tasks arrive. The authors derive regret bounds for the algorithm, giving a theoretical analysis of sequential transfer in this setting. The contribution formalizes how estimating recurring task models can be incorporated into an online decision procedure.
neurips-2013-sequential-transfer-in-mult.tldr: A bandit algorithm estimates a finite set of task models to transfer experience sequentially, with regret bounds for its performance.

paragraphs: Association field models describe relationships among image edges and have been used to explain human contour grouping and patterns of long-range connections in visual cortex. These models largely rely on pairwise edge statistics from natural scenes. This paper asks whether relationships between pairs capture enough of the structure relevant to these explanations.

The authors develop a spectral test for the sufficiency of pairwise statistics. The test reveals significant higher-order structure, showing that the organization of edges contains information beyond the pairwise description. This finding motivates examining how larger combinations of edges contribute to the patterns that association fields are intended to represent.

An analysis based on probabilistic spectral embedding identifies components of the association field that depend on curvature. Curvature therefore emerges as part of the richer statistical organization uncovered by the analysis. The findings also pose a challenge for biological learning algorithms: accounts of how these structures are learned must address the higher-order organization that the paper identifies, alongside familiar pairwise relationships.
neurips-2013-third-order-edge-statistics.tldr: A spectral analysis reveals higher-order, curvature-dependent edge structure beyond the pairwise statistics underlying association field models.

paragraphs: Experimental findings from one environment may be useful in another, but differences between environments complicate that transfer. This paper studies how to combine findings from several heterogeneous domains to estimate causal effects in a target environment where only limited experiments can be conducted. The available evidence includes both observations and experiments spread across domains.

The authors translate transportability questions into symbolic derivations using do-calculus, a formal system for reasoning about interventions. This extends treatment of transportability based on full experiments to settings with restricted experimental scope and multiple sources. The approach makes the reasoning about which evidence can be transferred an explicit part of constructing an estimate.

The paper provides graphical and algorithmic conditions for computing a transport formula. Such a formula specifies how information from the different domains can be combined to obtain a consistent estimate of the desired effect. The contribution is a formal route to evidence fusion when the relevant conditions hold, addressing differences between environments and limits on experimentation within the same framework.
neurips-2013-transportability-from-multi.tldr: Do-calculus provides conditions and formulas for combining evidence across heterogeneous environments when experiments are limited.
